item.title: Salvage Company Hoping to Sell Titanic Artifacts Challenges Court’s Role
item.description:
For much of the past four decades, the company that owns exclusive salvage rights to the Titanic shipwreck had vowed it would not sell the artifacts or break up the full collection.

But earlier this year, the company — the Atlanta-based R.M.S. Titanic Inc. — made plans to auction off 100 of the 5,500 artifacts it has collected. It went to court on Thursday to defend the proposed sale.

In U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Va., the company argued before Judge Rebecca Beach Smith that she has no jurisdiction over the 100 disputed artifacts because they were recovered in 1987 and were awarded to the company by a French court.

Under maritime law, salvage claims of wrecks in international waters can be taken to any admiralty court in the world. R.M.S. Titanic initially took its 1987 claim to France, but it brought claims for items salvaged later to the federal court in Norfolk, which is home to many maritime law firms.

The hearing also touched on R.M.S. Titanic’s financial condition. In court papers, the company has said it was suffering financially and needed to sell the 100 artifacts to pay debts and raise money to conserve and curate the remaining artifacts.

Judge Smith questioned the severity of the financial problems, noting that R.M.S. Titanic is backed by wealthy institutions. “Why do you need to sell these artifacts?” she asked.

The company’s lawyer, Brian Wainger, responded that “R.M.S.T. is in financial straits.”

Judge Smith also heard arguments from the U.S. government, which opposes the sale. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration argues that R.M.S. Titanic is bound by legal promises to keep the collection intact and never to sell items to private collectors.

Judge Smith did not rule on Thursday but is expected to issue a written opinion in the coming weeks.

The Titanic sank on its maiden voyage after hitting an iceberg on April 14, 1912. The wreck lies on the ocean floor, two and a half miles below the surface, about 400 miles off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada.

From the very start, the work of salvaging the wreck, which began in 1987, has been controversial. Critics call it grave robbing. Supporters say it is a way of honoring the 1,500 people who died on that fateful night by using the artifacts to tell their stories.

The Norfolk federal court granted R.M.S. Titanic exclusive salvage rights to the Titanic in 1994. The company has raised 5,500 artifacts from the wreck site in seven expeditions from 1987 to 2004. About 1,800 of those artifacts were raised in the first expedition, in 1987, and it is some of those 1987 artifacts that are now the subject of dispute.

To date, the company has not sold any Titanic artifacts, though it proposed the sale of some in 2016. It has instead made money from public exhibitions of the artifacts that have drawn more than 35 million visitors worldwide. The company has permanent exhibitions in Las Vegas and Orlando and has five traveling shows that are currently in Cleveland; Portland, Ore.; Germany; Poland; and the Czech Republic.

Through the years, the company has experienced financial difficulties. It emerged from bankruptcy in 2019, under new ownership, and is currently being sued for more than $4 million by a contractor.

In recent court papers, R.M.S. Titanic said it “continues to face financial difficulties and has experienced significant operating losses,” but it did not specify why it was losing money or the amount of losses.

In a recent court filing, the company listed the 100 artifacts that it wants to sell, including a bronze cherub statue from the ship’s Grand Staircase, a bell from the ship’s crow’s nest, a diamond pendant necklace, a safe, a pocket watch, a ship steward’s shirt and other personal items from passengers and crew members, including jewelry, coins and bank notes.

The company originally planned to announce the artifact auction in April, but Judge Smith stopped any marketing or sale until she could determine the company’s legal rights.

In its original auction plan, R.M.S. Titanic proposed a four-city worldwide tour of the artifacts to attract possible buyers, including “V.I.P.-access previews” for what it described as institutional clients, major collectors, museum curators and the media.

To date, the court has received 18 letters from individuals and organizations in the United States and Europe opposing the sale, but no letters in favor of the sale. One group, the International Congress of Maritime Museums, representing 250 museums around the world, wrote that there is “overwhelming consensus” among its members that the sale should not proceed, and if it does, “none of our member museums would agree to exhibit the material” that would be sold from the collection.

The government of France also sent a letter to the U.S. State Department expressing “deep concern and opposition” to the auction plan. The 1987 artifacts were raised from the Titanic wreck site in a joint American-French expedition, and a French court gave R.M.S. Titanic title to those artifacts.

The French Embassy wrote that selling those items would violate a promise the company made to France in 1993 never to sell or break up the artifact collection, except for exhibition purposes.

The Norfolk court has allowed R.M.S. Titanic Inc. to retrieve artifacts from the ocean floor around the wreck, but the company has not been allowed to cut into the wreck or detach objects from the ship itself.

Since 2004, the company has not salvaged any additional artifacts, but it did conduct scientific expeditions in 2010 and 2024.

item.title: Kalshi Ordered to Cease Most Operations in Washington State
item.description:
A judge in Seattle has barred Kalshi from most operations in Washington State, the latest legal blow to prediction markets as states enforce existing gambling laws.

The state’s attorney general sued Kalshi in King County Superior Court in March, arguing that the platform was operating illegally in Washington, which prohibits online sports betting.

Judge John McHale ruled in a preliminary injunction on Wednesday that the company was breaking state laws that have tightly regulated gambling since 1889. He ordered Kalshi to stop allowing Washington residents to place bets on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science — the bulk of the platform’s offerings.

The state’s attorney general, Nick Brown, said in a statement on Thursday, “As this case moves forward, we will continue to enforce Washington law and hold Kalshi accountable for misleading consumers.”

A Kalshi spokesperson said in a statement that the platform disagreed with the decision and was considering its legal options. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal regulator of prediction markets, has “exclusive jurisdiction over our exchange,” the spokesperson added.

Washington is the latest state to challenge the operation of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket, which have grown rapidly and transformed into cultural phenomena. Prediction markets allow people to wager on everything from college football games to who will win on “The Traitors.”

The companies have attracted billions of dollars in trades, but their popularity has prompted more than a dozen states that restrict gambling to pursue legal action.

New York’s attorney general sued Kalshi late last month, accusing the company of operating illegally. Minnesota lawmakers passed a law banning the apps outright this year, although a judge has put that ban on pause.

In July, Nevada became the first state to force Kalshi to restrict users from wagering on sports, elections and entertainment.

Prediction markets and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission have fought back hard in court, arguing that prediction markets are regulated at the federal level and that states have no legal authority over them.

When Washington sued Kalshi, the state pointed out that the company’s advertisements appeared to acknowledge the illicit nature of the app. One Kalshi ad showed someone texting, “I found a way to bet on the NFL even though we live in Washington.”

In July, Judge McHale found that Kalshi’s advertising was deceptive and that the company most likely violated the state’s gambling laws and consumer protections.

As part of the court order on Wednesday, Kalshi is barred from advertising to Washington consumers. The order also requires the company to impose a preliminary form of geofencing, a technology that creates a virtual boundary on the app, by next Wednesday and a more effective version by Sept. 2.

item.title: How Pennsylvania Got Hooked on Games That Look a Lot Like Slot Machines
item.description:
For the past 12 years in Pennsylvania, a new kind of game has proliferated in gas stations and laundromats across the state. It looks a lot like a slot machine but, legally speaking, has not been considered one.

The games — tall, colorful terminals where players insert cash and set wagers, setting off bright, spinning graphics — are instead called “skill games.”

They’re called this because if you lose a spin, you can recoup your money by playing a long, tedious game of memory, thus introducing an element of “skill.” And games of skill for prizes, like a claw machine, aren’t considered gambling. Here’s how it works:

The operation of a skill game is so similar to that of a normal slot machine that it’s not always obvious what the memory game is, or how to access it.

Tapping this message reveals an extended matching game that, if completed successfully, recoups the user’s wager plus an additional 5 percent.

Tapping this message reveals an extended matching game that, if completed successfully, recoups the user’s wager plus an additional 5 percent.

In Allentown, Pa., we played a memory game from Pace-O-Matic that took 9 minutes 50 seconds to complete, earning 3 cents of profit.

In other words, the game seems engineered to make the benefits of playing the memory game not worth the time or energy it takes to beat it — if a player even notices the game in the first place.

In June, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that skill games could not be distinguished from slot machines, and so could no longer be set up anywhere without a gambling license. But the court gave a 120-day grace period before the ban takes effect, and both Democrats and Republicans in the state Legislature are racing to pass laws that would save them.

The conundrum now facing Pennsylvania is part of the rapid expansion of legal gambling and gambling-like behavior across the country, from sports betting to prediction markets. The state now has an estimated 70,000 skill game terminals scattered around grocery stores, V.F.W. halls, pizza shops, bowling alleys, tanning salons, cigar lounges, hotel lobbies, barber shops, farmers markets, strip clubs and car towing garages.

Does the state let the court decision stand, leading to the removal of what will now be illegal gambling machines? Or does it fully legalize and regulate them, boosting tax revenue — and the state budget — while preserving valuable income for thousands of small businesses?

Pennsylvania’s skill game boom started in 2014 when Pace-O-Matic introduced its first machine to include the optional memory mini-game. The machines survived several lawsuits and seizures when lower courts ruled that the memorization aspect made them predominantly games of skill. Other manufacturers soon came up with their own copycat versions.

Kris Allan runs a vending machine company that installs and maintains the machines at no upfront cost in exchange for a split of the revenue. He says the highest-performing businesses are restaurants or bars, which often gross as much as $5,000 a month from the skill games. He also leases machines to laundromats, which generally don’t make as much, according to Mr. Allan, though he said he knows one that grosses about $8,000 a month from the games.

In Allentown, we visited five laundromats, all of which had skill games. We talked to several customers playing them while they waited for their clothes to dry. Most had never played the memorization portion of the skill game and assumed it was called a “skill” game because it takes skill to know when a machine is “hot” and ready to dispense a jackpot.

We also went to Big Valley Game Room, a strip-mall business in Allentown offering solely skill games. Dan Blount, a 71-year-old customer, said he did not know the distinction between slot machines and skill games.

“When you keep saying ‘skill games,’ it’s throwing me off,” he said. Though he plays the machines “every other day,” he didn’t know the memory game existed. “I lose 40, 50 bucks and then I’m gone,” he said.

Josh Ercole, executive director of the Council on Compulsive Gambling of Pennsylvania, said it’s hard to gauge the scope of skill-game addiction because many people who call the council’s hotline may refer to skill games as slot machines. Still, his agency’s data lists a ninefold increase between 2019 and 2025 of people who specifically reported skill games as their primary addictive gambling behavior.

“Regardless of what the legal system decides to assign as far as a name, there’s a lot of people that are struggling,” he said.

Cherelle Parker, mayor of Philadelphia, applauded the court decision classifying skill games as gambling devices. She said in a statement that skill games were “predatory” and that they should be allowed only in private clubs and casinos.

But state politicians have been much more reluctant to favor a ban. Gov. Josh Shapiro has come out against an outright ban, saying the games should be regulated and taxed. (Profits from ordinary slot machines in Pennsylvania, located in regulated casinos, are taxed at 33 percent or more.)

Gene Yaw, a Republican state senator, is co-sponsor of bipartisan legislation to regulate and tax the games. He said legalizing them would also help protect jobs manufacturing the games, including those of a large game maker in his district.

Mr. Yaw’s regulation would add age minimums to the machine and permit them only in stores that already have age-check procedures for products (a bar would be allowed to have them, but not a carwash). The bill would also ban businesses that operate exclusively to offer skill games (several call themselves “Skill-sinos”).

Danilo Burgos, a Democratic state representative, has proposed his own competing legislation to regulate and tax the games. He said he was a proponent of “expanding the tax base” and blames influence from the traditional gambling industry for slowing new laws that would legalize the games and increase competition.

“You have all the lobbyists from Wall Street that don’t want Main Street, Pa., to be able to participate in this wealth transfer,” Mr. Burgos said.

Other states clamped down on skill games before they grew ubiquitous. Virginia and Kentucky passed legislation to ban skill games after they became increasingly popular in local gas stations and convenience stores. And Texas’ attorney general, Ken Paxton, recently issued an opinion saying skill games fit the definition of gambling because chance plays a role.

Jim DeLisio, owner of the Racehorse Tavern in Thomasville, Pa., has three skill machines in his bar that he places next to his Pennsylvania Lottery vending machines. He said the machines were a “godsend” to small businesses like his during the pandemic, and he’s hoping regulation passes with moderate taxes. He also said skill games should be permitted only in locations that already check for age identification.

“I’ve been in stores where you have little kids sitting at them thinking they’re a video game,” he said. “They’re excited. It’s all the different colors and this and that. Everybody and their brother is building them and nobody seems to be regulating them one way or the other.”

item.title: A Silicon Valley Dirt Farmer Hangs Up His Shears
item.description:
When Andy Mariani’s parents tended their orchards in the Santa Clara Valley nearly a century ago, the region was known as the Valley of Heart’s Delight. Blenheim apricots, Bing and Royal Ann cherries and French prunes with pink and white blossoms bejeweled the land.

Silicon eventually replaced the delight. But as crops gave way to computer chips and multimillion-dollar homes sprouted on former family farms, some 60 acres of the Mariani land remained stubbornly fruiting.

But not for much longer. If Santa Clara County officials approve, Andy’s Orchard, which sits on land his family purchased in 1957, will be sold. Mr. Mariani’s 7,000 trees will be uprooted and replaced with hundreds of homes, two parks, a playground and pickleball courts. Now 80, Mr. Mariani says his once profitable orchard is no longer sustainable.

“It’s time,” he said. “I have hardly any money in the bank.” He relies on Social Security payments.

Mr. Mariani’s 280 varieties of stone fruit, chosen for flavor, not shelf life, are cherished in the region. Hundreds attend his summertime tastings. At the Santa Monica Farmers’ Market, customers line up at 4:30 a.m. for the orchard’s Baby Crawford peaches, Greengage plums and Black Republican cherries. David Karp, a noted fruit writer, calls him “the Picasso of stone fruit.” Mélisse Restaurant, with two Michelin stars, serves wedges of Mariani’s Arctic Jay white nectarines unadorned on crushed ice at the end of a 20-course tasting menu.

“We always, always, always go to Andy’s Orchard,” said Ken Takayama, the restaurant’s co-chef. “The first time I tried a nectarine they produced, it was as if I never tasted a nectarine before.”

Mr. Mariani’s fruit is best eaten over the kitchen sink.

Or right from the tree. “When you’re out in the orchard,” he said, “you don’t worry about the juice.”

When he was young, Mr. Mariani plucked fruit in the orchard next to his family’s house, where he still lives. He learned grafting and other farming techniques from his father, who, along with his mother and two oldest siblings, emigrated in the 1930s from the island of Vis, now a part of Croatia.

Mr. Mariani remembers a seminal moment in his childhood when he tasted a peach his father had grown by grafting an early Crawford peach onto an apricot tree. “I spent my whole lifetime trying to bring back that flavor and relive that joy,” he said.

His older brothers were expected to operate the orchard. Andy got a master’s in public administration. But at 23, he was diagnosed with a rare, debilitating autoimmune disease. He quit work as assistant city manager in a nearby town, and for years suffered at home. Experimental medications eventually helped, and when he was 40, the disease went into remission.

“Because of that illness I had, I almost died, and I thought, I want to enjoy my life,” Mr. Mariani said.

He returned to the orchard.

In his search for fruit that is sweet, acidic and aromatic, he digs through old nursery catalogs, visits backyard collectors, university collections and obscure nurseries. In Tashkent, Uzbekistan, a botanist gave him two seeds from golden yellow nectarines. He planted and replanted seeds, selecting the best strain, which became his Silk Road nectarines.

He rescued a peach that the University of California, Davis, had rejected for being too small and delicate for commercial use. Mr. Mariani tasted in it the exotic flavor of his father’s Crawford peach. He named the new fruit Baby Crawford, which became his most popular peach.

As Mr. Mariani farmed, his orchard became increasingly locked in. Technology companies like Hewlett-Packard, Apple, Google and Meta grew, and so did the population. In 1950, when Mr. Mariani was 5, Santa Clara County had 290,547 residents. Today, it has 1.9 million, and a raging demand for housing. Urbanization and farming are incompatible, Mr. Mariani said.

Deer and squirrels dine on his fruit. He also copes with an invasive fruit fly, an insidious oak root fungus and “catastrophic climate change,” he said. This winter’s inadequate chill resulted in almost no Baby Crawford peaches or cherries, his largest and traditionally most profitable crop.

Farming Mr. Mariani’s way is expensive. “If you grow one variety on 30 acres, you have one method of thinning, pruning and irrigation,” he said. But with so many varieties, cultivation must be customized.

Some trees must be picked every other day for two weeks, said Jose Garcia, Mr. Mariani’s foreman. “Sometimes if the fruit turns yellow that doesn’t mean it’s ripe,” he said. “You have to taste it.”

Mr. Garcia earns $24 an hour and is one of about 15 workers who live rent-free on the farm. All but the newest hires earn above the California minimum wage, Mr. Mariani said. Few work full time. Most have side jobs. Mr. Garcia, with Mr. Mariani’s encouragement, attended college and started a maintenance business.

For decades, family farms have been disappearing as corporate farms with lower pricing have expanded and young people find jobs elsewhere.

“Aging farmers are met with an alternative of developing their land or going broke,” said Julie F. Morris, the Santa Clara County agricultural liaison. Unlike soybeans, corn and wheat, she said, specialty fruit is not subsidized by the federal government. “The fact that we are losing the land and conditions that create those Blenheim apricots is a tragedy.”

“Blenheim apricots are so delicate you can hardly take them across the street without their falling apart,” said Mitch Mariani, Andy’s older brother, who farms 12 acres. Andy’s Orchard is one of the few remaining farms that grow the once plentiful fruit.

For generations, farmers grew fruit in this region with its alluvial soil, sun-punched summers and cool winters. At midcentury, an estimated 109,000 acres were orchards; fewer than 4,000 acres remain.

While other family orchards sold chunks of land to keep their farms going, Mr. Mariani survived by operating a country store where he sells fruit, chocolate-dipped dried apricots and jams. He also sells wholesale to high-end specialty markets.

He calls himself a “dirt farmer,” which he says is a farmer who earns all his income from farming, as opposed to a “gentleman farmer,” who has money from other sources. Now he is joining their ranks.

After a decade of losses, Mr. Mariani agreed with his brother to sell the farm. He never married and has no offspring. And no one in the younger Mariani generation wants to operate a failing business.

Mana Investments, a California real estate investment firm, has an option to buy what it calls the Mariani Ranch, with plans to build 376 homes. Mr. Mariani and his brother won’t discuss the terms of the offer.

Scott Murray, a Mana Investments partner, said that “at a minimum” one acre that “is ready to break ground is worth a million dollars.” When the project is completed, Mana Investments anticipates revenue of $600 million. An environmental impact report is expected to be completed within a year.

Mr. Mariani expects that some orchard workers will return to their families in Mexico and that others will attend school or search for work. And he will move out of the family homestead to a friend’s house in town.

“I’m for preserving agriculture,” he said, “but not where it’s no longer viable.” He will continue farming on 20 acres of leased land.

Still, he said, the demise of Andy’s Orchard will be “heartbreaking.” At this year’s final tasting, as Mr. Mariani sat in a weathered chair near the tasting tables, a young boy called out, “Thank you, Andy, for growing amazing fruit!”

Mr. Mariani applauded. He was reminded of his first taste of his father’s Crawford peach. “That’s what I’ll miss,” he said. “I’m trying to give kids the same experience I got.”

item.title: Gone in 20 Minutes: Half-Off Sushi Draws Throngs to New York’s Japanese Markets
item.description:
On a warm Thursday this summer, the line began to form around 7:45 p.m. inside a small shop in Manhattan. Customers snaked through the aisles, small bounties in hand. Soon, more than 50 people were packed into the store, waiting for the clock to strike 8.

They weren’t chasing the latest viral food craze, or a merch drop from an indie fashion brand.

They wanted sushi, and they wanted it for 50 percent off.

New Yorkers have gotten used to waiting in is-it-even-worth-it lines for meals and shelling out $20 for a salad or a smoothie. But at a proliferating assortment of East Asian grocery chains selling fresh Japanese meals, city dwellers and visitors may have at last found a true bargain.

That is, if they're willing to wait until 8 p.m. for half-off sushi, sashimi and onigiri.

“In New York City, it’s a great deal,” said Jodie Goldberg, 34, who had arrived at Ten Ichi Mart — which has locations in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens — around 7:40 p.m. and had several packaged rolls in her basket.

“In a world full of places that are trying to scam you, not Ten Ichi Mart after eight,” she added.

The scene inside the Ten Ichi Mart is repeated nightly at similar stores — Hashi Market, Sakura Market, Genkiya Mart and others — most nights of the week.

The crowd gathers. The cashier motions. The procession begins.

As the customers at the front check out, people in the back of the line, some spilling into the street, grab what remains from the refrigerated shelves. The products, fresh throughout the day, would find their fate at the bottom of a trash can should they not be sold before closing time.

To get the best sushi and nigiri, you have to get there early.

The sushi is not what you’d find at omakase counters where you might spend hundreds of dollars. But some of the stores prepare the sushi just for the evening crowd because it’s become so popular. Hungry New Yorkers spend $6 on a package of spicy crunchy salmon that would have cost $12 minutes before.

Sushi has transitioned from its 1980s mystique in America to becoming a staple. A sushi dinner from a restaurant may remain pricey — at the popular restaurant Sugarfish, where diners wait more than an hour to be seated, the cheapest meal costs $34.

Many American diners are willing to enjoy convenient, no-frills Japanese-inspired meals from all manner of grocers.

That’s called retail sushi, or “deli sushi.” Last year it was one of the fastest-growing products in supermarkets, according to the research firm Circana. In 2024, retail sushi was a $2.8 billion business, up 7 percent from 2023, according to Circana. In 2025, the Kroger supermarket chain said sales were up to a million rolls per day.

But not every store offers the discounts that attract throngs of customers.

Bill Chen, a manager of Ten Ichi Mart, which opened its first location in 2021, said that sushi was being tossed overnight before the store began the promotion. “It ended up getting popular,” he said. “We make sushi just for the promotion.”

The discount sales are hard to give up, he said. Mr. Chen said that the company breaks even on the meals but people placing drinks or snacks in their baskets while they wait help the business.

The dynamic is similar at Hashi Market, which will soon open its seventh outlet. The discount at some of its stores is only 30 percent.

“We were even thinking of not doing that promotion anymore because the margin is really thin,” said Ava Liu, the head of operations. “But people are looking for it. They wait to buy the sushi, so it’s hard for us to say we can’t.”

Most sushi is, after all, raw, so do customers need to rush home with their spicy tuna or tamago nigiri?

“The longer you hold the food, potentially the riskier it is,” said Donald Schaffner, chair of the department of food science at Rutgers University. “But if that sushi has been properly refrigerated, then it should be OK.”

At the back of the Ten Ichi Mart line, Paul Luyton, 20, a French tourist who seldom eats sushi back home, held a box of salmon avocado rolls. His partner, next to him in line, had told him about the discount.

“She told me this week we need to go to get sushi,” Mr. Luyton said. “She saw it on TikTok, the sushi, and it looked nice.”

Rachel Chen, 29, held a package of yellowtail-jalapeño and salmon sushi. She said that she takes advantage of the deal three times a month when she gets out of work later than usual.

If the line gets too long, she said, it’s not worth the wait.

By about 8:20 p.m. most nights, the only sign that a line of sushi gourmands had ever existed at many of the stores is a barren refrigerator.

It awaits the next day’s bounty, and a queue of deal-seeking New Yorkers eager to eat.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.
